title: The Implicit Bias of Depth: From Neural Collapse to Softmax Codes
claim: A configuration with a smaller angle between features can still achieve larger Euclidean separation if it lies on a larger-radius sphere.
layout: single 2-D plot, vectors from origin, nested semicircles, dashed separation chords
description: A single matplotlib-style 2-D plot with gridlines and numeric axes. It shows two nested black semicircles centered at the origin, a smaller one with radius about 0.097 and a larger one with radius about 0.177. From the origin, thick black arrows point to the upper-left and upper-right of each semicircle. The inner pair is labeled μ_DNC and μ'_DNC. The outer pair is labeled μ_LR and μ'_LR. The outer arrows are steeper, so the angle between them is smaller. A blue dashed horizontal line joins each pair of arrow tips. The outer dashed line is clearly longer than the inner one. The eye goes first to the long blue dashed chord at the top, then to the arrows and the two nested arcs. The figure shows that the low-rank geometry gets more Euclidean separation than DNC despite its smaller angle.
caption: Illustration of low-rank bias for $K=4,L=3,n=1$, with all parameter matrices normalized to unit Frobenius norm. $\mu_{DNC}, \mu_{DNC}'$ denote two feature embeddings of a logit matrix $Z$ under DNC, while $\mu_{LR}, \mu_{LR}'$ denote two feature embeddings of a logit matrix $Z$ under the low-rank geometry of Eq. [ref]. Although DNC yields the larger angle between features, the low-rank geometry lies on a large-radius hypersphere and therefore attains a larger Euclidean separation.
abstract: Neural collapse (NC) describes the structured geometry that emerges in the features and weights of trained classifiers. Recent theory suggests NC can be suboptimal in deep architectures, attributing this to an explicit low-rank bias from L2 regularization. We study the deep unconstrained feature model (UFM)-equivalent to a deep linear network with orthogonal inputs-trained without regularization, to isolate how gradient descent and depth alone shape NC. We show that depth induces an implicit low-rank bias: low-rank matrices propagate norm more efficiently through successive multiplications, promoting low-rank alternatives to NC. These alternatives, we argue, correspond to softmax codes: max-margin solutions previously found in width-bottlenecked networks. Analyzing training dynamics under spectral initialization, we identify an early-time repulsion among singular values that drives low-rank emergence, and characterize how depth shrinks NC's basin of attraction. Finally, we show that some effects act in the opposite direction: for randomly initialized networks, increasing width biases training toward higher-rank solutions. Our results provide the first asymptotic and dynamic characterization of implicit bias in deep UFMs trained with unregularized multiclass cross-entropy.
